copy.title: From Model Output to Physical Action: Evidence and Authority Gates for Agentic AI
copy.one_line_summary: A practical systems pattern for keeping tool-using AI agents useful without letting unsupported model confidence silently become consequential action.
copy.abstract:
Agentic AI becomes a different engineering problem once model output can modify state, operate tools, or trigger physical work. In those settings, the most important failure is not simply a wrong answer: it is a plausible answer acquiring authority it has not earned.

This session presents a practical systems pattern developed through Hardware-Splicer, an agentic hardware-engineering environment built around a strict separation between model reasoning and independently authoritative state. The agent can inspect evidence, reason, propose changes, and use engineering tools, while deterministic constraints, exact revision state, provenance-bearing evidence, and scoped human authorization remain outside the model.

Using adversarial hardware cases involving partial evidence, component-identity conflict, tool failure, plausible wrong analogy, and stale revisions, the talk shows how to design for failure instead of assuming perfect model behavior. The focus is on reusable production principles: fail closed on unresolved evidence, invalidate authority when revisions change, distinguish reasoning from verified state, preserve traceability, and measure abstention, recovery, false blocking, intervention, and useful task completion—not only successful answers.

Hardware-Splicer is the concrete case study, but the architecture generalizes to other consequential agent workflows where an AI system can act rather than merely advise.
takeaways: Reasoning and authority should be separate system concepts. A model proposal should not automatically become verified state or permission to act.
Evidence must be bound to identity and revision. Stale, conflicting, or incomplete evidence should invalidate authority rather than silently carry forward.
Production agent evaluation needs failure metrics. Abstention, recovery, false blocking, intervention, and unauthorized action attempts matter as much as task completion.
copy.speaker_bio: Christopher Ongko is a master's researcher at Yuan Ze University working on evidence-governed agentic systems, research-data infrastructure, and empirical research. His current technical work includes Hardware-Splicer, a model-independent environment for bounded AI-assisted hardware engineering, and research systems focused on provenance and reproducibility. His recurring research interest is how AI systems can remain useful while maintaining explicit boundaries between model inference, evidence, verified state, and consequential authority.
copy.short_bio: Christopher Ongko is a Yuan Ze University master's researcher building evidence-governed agentic and research-data systems. His work focuses on keeping model inference, evidence, revision state, and consequential authority explicitly separated in real AI workflows.
session_flow: Why tool-using agents create a new failure boundary.
Hardware-Splicer as a concrete case study.
Four-layer pattern: model reasoning → deterministic constraints → provenance/revision evidence → human authority.
Adversarial cases and what goes wrong.
Metrics for abstention, recovery, false blocking, intervention, and useful completion.
Generalization to production agentic systems beyond hardware.
nonclaims: Do not claim AWS services are currently part of Hardware-Splicer unless that becomes true.
Do not claim a live external model has already passed the frozen corpus.
Do not claim fresh physical correctness is already closed.
Do not present the system as a universally safe agent.
